title: Showcase: the reveal
summary: They hand the finished build to its person, recipient in the room, give the science fair talk exactly as the fair will hear it, then close the season with the review and the patch ceremony.
materials: the finished free build, tested and wrapped or covered
the science fair board from week 11
the Maker's Log, bug diary and budget sheet
the free build idea page with the circled name
the fix-it kit the bug diary suggests: tape, glue, a spare part, a charger
the person the build is for, in the room or on a call
a sheet of card and coloured pens for the season 2 patch

steps.title: Reveal day
steps.body:
The idea page opened in week 1. The person was named in week 8. The pitch, the budget, the walls, the bug diary, the interview, the test, the one improvement: all of it walked here. Today you hand the finished build to the person it was made for, and give the science fair talk exactly as the fair will hear it.

Run the day in this order: the last pit lane, the handover, the talk, then the season ceremony. The design loop has one honest step left, and it is the one that scares builders a little every time: deliver. A build on your desk is a project; a build in their hands is a gift, and a gift is a promise that the thing works.

One planning note before anything: the recipient belongs in the room. If they truly cannot be there, plan the recorded handover on purpose, camera up, their face on a call, treated as the show it is and not a lesser copy. Decide which it will be now, before the rehearsal.

And if the real science fair has a date, say it out loud today and mark where the board will wait for it. This talk is not practice for the fair; it is the fair's opening night.

Five minutes on your typing site while the stage settles. Type the four words of your board, five times each, without looking down: question, plan, trials, result. Then type the sentence that runs the whole day, twice: I made this for you, and I tested it.

steps.title: Why the handover is the real test
steps.body:
All season the same truth kept coming back: the test you never tuned for is the only test that counts. The robot proved it on the family's secret course in week 8, and today your build faces its own version: real life in the recipient's hands, on their ordinary days, without you standing next to it.

Engineers have a word for today: shipping. A thing is shipped when the person it is for can use it without its builder in the room. Shipping is why real teams test with real users, write instructions, and put handles where hands actually go. It is also why the moment of handover feels big to every builder alive: after it, the build answers for itself.

So watch closely what happens after you let go. Where the build fits their life straight away, your week 10 interview did its work: you heard them right. Where they hold it strangely or ask how do I, you have found the gap between the user in your head and the person in the room. Week 11's improvement came from exactly one such gap. Builders who ship learn where their guesses about people run out, and that lesson does not live on any workbench.

figure.alt: The staged showcase table: the wrapped build in the centre, the science fair board standing to one side, the Maker's Log, bug diary and budget sheet laid out nearby, and a fix-it kit of tape, glue, a spare part and a charger within reach. A note says the talk was rehearsed once with a timer before showtime, and the handover sentence naming why this build for this person is ready.

items.s: Rehearse the talk once, timer running, board up
Handover sentence ready: why this build, for this person

steps.title: The last pit lane
steps.body:
A showman tests the machine the same day as the show, and today that rule is sacred. Run the whole build once, start to finish, the way the recipient will actually use it. If it has batteries, make them fresh. If it has code, start it from power-off once, not from a lucky warm start. If it moves, folds, pours or holds, do the motion with your own hands.

Pack the fix-it kit: the two or three things your bug diary says this build reaches for. Tape, glue, a spare part, the charger. The diary knows your build's weak knee better than anyone; trust its record.

Stage the show: build wrapped or covered, board standing where the talk will happen, Maker's Log, bug diary and budget sheet on the table for the ceremony later. Then rehearse the talk once, alone, out loud, timer running, board up: question, plan, trials, result, with the week 11 improvement in its place.

Last, decide the handover's one sentence: why this build, for this person, in words you actually heard from them in the week 10 interview. Write it on a card if you might wobble. It is the first sentence of the show.
checklist: The whole build ran once today, start to finish, the way they will use it
The fix-it kit is packed from what the bug diary says this build reaches for
The board is staged and the talk was rehearsed once, out loud, with the timer
The handover sentence is ready: why this build, for this person

steps.title: The handover
steps.body:
Bring the person in. Say the one sentence, then put the build in their hands and step back. Their hands, not yours: the same rule the robot taught you in week 8. If they fumble, wait. An owner is allowed to find their own way into a gift, and where their hands go tells you the truth about your design.

Show them one thing only: the improvement their week 11 reaction bought. Name it plainly: you found this rough spot when you tried it, so I changed it, and here is what it does now. That sentence is the whole season's engineering in miniature: test, listen, improve.

Then it is theirs. Not on loan for the fair, theirs; the board and the photos carry the fair from here. If something breaks in their hands today, that is a bug diary moment in front of an audience: say what you expected, say what happened instead, and fix it calmly if the fix is small. A builder who repairs a gift with steady hands impresses harder than a builder whose gift never dared to be used.

Stay for their questions. The interview taught you to listen without defending; the handover is the graduation exam of exactly that skill.
checklist: I said the one sentence, then their hands held it, not mine
I waited through the first fumble without taking it back
The week 11 improvement was named, along with what their reaction taught me
It is theirs now, and I answered their questions without once defending

steps.title: The fair talk, opening night
steps.body:
Stand by the board and give the talk exactly as the fair will hear it: question, plan, trials, result. The family plays judge, the week 11 way: after the talk each person asks one skeptical question, and you answer from your trials, your bug diary and your budget sheet, never from hope.

Keep the talk inside its time. The week 11 rehearsal set your length; hold it tonight. If the fair has a rule sheet, obey all of it today, board size, time limit, everything, so opening night and fair night are the same show.

One rule for the answers: when a question finds something you did not test, say so plainly and say how you would test it. Judges, like families, trust a builder who knows the edge of their own evidence. You have been practising that sentence since week 1: this claim I tested, that one I would need to test.
checklist: The talk ran exactly as the fair will hear it, board up, inside its time
Question, plan, trials and result each got their moment, with the improvement in its place
Every skeptical question got an answer from evidence, or an honest here is how I would test it
The board is stored safe for the real fair

steps.title: Season review and the patch ceremony
steps.body:
Clear the table and lay the season on it: the perfboard gate badge from week 5, the adder photo or the breadboard itself, the mBot creature, the science fair board, and the free build idea page with its circled name. One sentence each, said to the family: what this one taught me.

Then retire the idea page with honours. Read out the ideas that never got built and save the page inside the Maker's Log: those are season 3 seeds, not losses. The page did its season's work, and the proof is sitting in someone's hands right now.

The patch ceremony closes it. Draw the season 2 patch together on card: the family decides what belongs on it, the coast, the creature, the gate, the gift, and everyone signs the back. Hang it where the family will pass it every day, and remember it is the first of its kind: season 3's will hang next to it.

Last word, one sentence from you: the thing I want to build next season. Say it to the room, write it inside the back cover of the Maker's Log, and close the book. Season 2 is shipped.
checklist: Every season artifact on the table got its one sentence
The idea page was read out, honoured and saved as season 3 seeds
The patch is drawn, signed and hanging on the wall it starts on
The next season sentence is said out loud and written in the back of the Maker's Log

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A video of the handover, from the one sentence to the moment the build lands in their hands, and the full fair talk with the board. End with a photo of the signed season 2 patch on the wall it starts on.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
